name: Valkey
model: Redis-compatible in-memory keys: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams; same commands and protocol as Redis 7.2
engine_note: Fork of Redis 7.2.4: in-memory hash table, command loop with multithreaded I/O, optional RDB snapshots and append-only file
consistency: Same as Redis: single commands atomic; MULTI/EXEC and scripts run without interleaving but do not roll back. Replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes can be lost on failover; WAIT is best effort. Replica reads can be stale.
scaling: Bigger machine; read replicas; Valkey Cluster shards keys automatically over 16384 hash slots, multi-key commands must stay in one slot.

licence_events.event: Linux Foundation launches Valkey, a BSD-3 fork of Redis 7.2.4, backed by AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, Ericsson and Snap, after Redis left BSD

version_note: 9.2.0-rc1 (2026-09-16) is a pre-release; 9.0.x and 8.x lines also still patched.
reach: Reach for it when you want a Redis-style cache, counter or queue under a permissive open source licence, or the default in-memory cache on AWS and Google Cloud.
avoid: Avoid when it would be the only copy of data you cannot lose, or when you need Redis 8 only features (built-in JSON, query engine, vector sets) by name.
escape: Postgres is too slow for per-request counters and caching at memory speed.
chat: Per-user rate-limit counters, session tokens, and a cache of recent chat messages.
notes: Valkey first release date taken from the 7.2.5 tag commit (2024-04-15, US Pacific; 2024-04-16 UTC). No Jepsen report on Valkey itself. Amazon MemoryDB is a Valkey/Redis-compatible service with a multi-AZ transaction log, so unlike plain Valkey it keeps acknowledged writes on failover; it is a separate product from ElastiCache. Redis 8 modules (JSON, search) are not part of Valkey core; Valkey has its own separate modules (valkey-json, valkey-search), not checked in detail.
